title: Flexible Space, Flexible Time: Engineering Students’ Inclusive Learning Conditions in Laboratory Classes
content: Purpose: This study examines how undergraduate engineering students experience spatial and temporal flexibility as part of the hidden infrastructure of inclusion, belonging, and academic performance in laboratory- and project-based engineering education. Design/methodology/approach: The study uses a mixed-methods analysis of an end-of-term self-reflection survey completed by 51 students. Descriptive statistics summarize closed-ended items on flexible lab formats, spatial flexibility, temporal flexibility, hybrid/asynchronous interest, and after-hours work. Open-ended responses were coded thematically to identify supports and desired environmental changes. Findings: Students valued embodied, in-person experimentation, but they did not frame inclusion as a simple preference for either face-to-face or online learning. Instead, the findings point to guided autonomy: functioning equipment, instructor/TA availability, clear procedural scaffolds, peer collaboration, and options for when and where portions of lab work are completed. Flexibility was strongest when it preserved hands-on practice while reducing unnecessary temporal, spatial, and cognitive friction. Originality: The paper reframes engineering laboratory inclusion as a spatial-temporal design problem rather than only a demographic representation problem. It offers a practical “flexible lab architecture” for equity-oriented laboratory pedagogy.
